extracted.intended_audience: indexers, copyeditors, publishers, and authors preparing indexes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and formatting back-of-book (and analogous electronic) indexes, including choice of terms, cross-references, entry style, numbering, alphabetization, and treatment of names and titles. Applicable to both print and electronic publication formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link index entries to text passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Index entries are best linked directly to the passage of text to which they refer; in works like this manual, links can be made directly to numbered paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in electronic publications, index entries should link to the actual passage (may be several screens beyond the first 'page'). This requires publisher/indexer intervention but improves reader experience. See EPUB specifications for detailed indexing support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive numbers formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Form for inclusive (continuing) page-number ranges should be consistent with the text and follow Chicago's traditional system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules (summary): Less than 100 — use all digits (3-10). 100 or multiples of 100 — use all digits (100-104). For many cases give only changed part: 101-8, 808-33, 321-28, 498-532, 1087-89, 1496-500, 11564-615, 12991-3001. Roman numerals always given in full. Use same form in index as in text. See en dash usage references (6.78) and other cross refs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references: general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-references come in two main kinds—see references and see also references—and are treated differently depending on whether they refer to a main heading or a subheading; use with discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set see and see also in italics (with specific exceptions); in electronic formats, cross-references should be linked. Overabundance of cross-references can irritate readers and may indicate need to consolidate entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: See references and double posting
rubrics_metrics.description: See references direct a reader from variant terms (informal to technical, pseudonym to real name, inverted to noninverted) to the full entry; double posting (listing page numbers under both headings) can be preferable when the full entry is about the same length as the see reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give see references where many readers might otherwise miss the full entry. Avoid see references that lead to another see (blind cross-reference). If duplication saves readers a trip, list page numbers under both headings (double posting). Examples: FBI -> Federal Bureau of Investigation vs Federal Bureau of Investigation. See 16.16 for notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: See references following a main heading (format)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a see reference follows a main heading it is preceded by a period and 'See' is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple see references are needed, arrange them alphabetically and separate by semicolons; they reflect capitalization and word order of the main heading.

rubrics_metrics.name: See references following a subheading (format)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a see reference follows a subheading it is put in parentheses and 'see' is lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies to run-in and indented indexes and to sub-subentries.

rubrics_metrics.name: See references to subheadings ('see under')
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cross-reference directs readers to a subentry under another main heading, use 'see under'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a 'see under' might fail to direct readers to the right spot, drop 'under' and add the wording of the subheading following a colon; the cross-reference wording must correspond exactly to the subheading for quick finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: See also references
rubrics_metrics.description: See also references are placed at the end of an entry when additional information can be found in another entry; formatted differently in run-in vs indented indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In run-in indexes they follow a period; in indented indexes they appear on a separate line. 'See also' is normally italicized and 'See' capitalized. Arrange multiple see also references alphabetically and separate with semicolons. Never lead a see also to a see reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between cross-references and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-referenced headings (and subheadings) should generally be cited in full, with capitalization, inversion, and punctuation exactly as in the heading referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long heading may occasionally be shortened if no confusion results, but consistency is required (e.g., 'See also Beethoven' if done consistently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic treatment of 'see' and 'see also'
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'see', 'see under', and 'see also' are normally italicized, with exceptions when what follows is italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If what follows (e.g., a book title) is italicized, set the words in roman to distinguish them; not necessary when they follow italics. Use roman when needed to avoid confusion with italicized items that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: See and see also may include generic references that refer to a type of heading rather than several specific headings; the entire cross-reference is then set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generic cross-references accompany specific ones, place the generic last (even if out of alphabetical order) and use 'and' following a semicolon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flush-and-hang (hanging-indent) formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexes are generally formatted in flush-and-hang (hanging-indent) style: first line flush left (main heading), following lines indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In print pubs, indexes usually set in multiple columns; in manuscripts, avoid columns. For subentries choose between run-in and indented styles depending on content (see 16.25, 16.26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of run-in versus indented style
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose run-in when space efficiency and single-level subentries prevail; choose indented when subentries (especially multiple levels) or scientific/reference works require clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago and many publishers prefer run-in because it takes less space; indented style is preferred in scientific/reference works and when sub-subentries are required. See examples in 16.26 and 16.27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run-in style specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: In run-in style, subentries follow the main entry on the same line separated by semicolons; if main heading is immediately followed by subentries, separate by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If main heading is immediately followed by locators, precede locators with a comma and end with semicolon. Works best with only one level of subentry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indented style specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: In indented (stacked) style each subentry begins a new line and is indented (usually one em); no colon before the first subheading and subentries are not separated by semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runover lines must be further indented (usually two ems) to distinguish from subentries and indentation is measured from the left margin. Cross-references belonging to the entry as a whole appear at the end of the list of subentries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-subentries in run-in indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid many sub-subentries in a run-in index; if a very few are needed, repeat keyword or indent subentries with an em dash and run in sub-subentries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sub-subentries are necessary, better to choose indented format. Em dashes are not used where only one level of subentry is needed. Examples provided for run-in treatment with em dash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-subentries in indented indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: In indented indexes, sub-subentries are best run in; if that makes the index hard to use, indent sub-subentries more deeply than subentries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When run-in sub-subentries are used, standard two-em runover indentation suffices; if deeper indentation is used, runover lines require three ems which may produce short lines. If sub-sub-subentries are needed, use style B and run them in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and usage must match the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Each index must reflect the style used in the work (spelling, diacritics, italics, punctuation, inclusive-number form, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If British spelling is used in text, use it in index. Preserve accents/diacritics as in text. Do not modernize older geographical terms. Only give cross-references when readers might not find information otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing indexing terms: follow author's usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording for headings should be concise and logical; choose terms according to the author's usage when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author uses 'essence' to mean 'being', index under 'essence' and provide a cross-reference from 'being'. An indexer unfamiliar with subject matter may ask author for essential terms. For journals use predetermined keywords or prior indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms that should not be indexed
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not index proper names, places, or terms that occur only in passing or are not essential to the work's theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist indexing scene-setting place-names or incidental individuals unless relevant to readers (vanity entries allowed occasionally). Index terms central to theme (e.g., MG sports car in an automobile history) should be indexed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing between variant names
rubrics_metrics.description: When proper names appear in more than one form or incompletely, decide which form to use as main entry and which as cross-reference; supply identifying information if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few indexes require biographical detail; use reference works for decisions. Prefer forms as they have become widely known, but respect variant spellings used in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing familiar forms of personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Full form of personal names should be indexed as they have become widely known; prefer the variant used in the text when it is preferred there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In works devoted to a person, the full form of the name should appear. Use bracketed editorial glosses sparingly to distinguish forms (examples: Cervantes, Miguel de [not Cervantes Saavedra, Miguel de]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing pseudonyms or stage names
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who used pseudonyms are usually listed under real names, unless the pseudonym is the household word—in which case use pseudonym as main entry and give real name in parentheses if relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references are seldom necessary when pseudonym is widely known. Examples: Ouida -> Ramée, M. L. de la (pseud. Ouida); but some forms like Molière (Jean-Baptiste Poquelin) presented differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing persons with the same name
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish persons with the same name by middle initial or parenthetical tag; use identifying tags when many persons with same last name occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Campbell, James; Campbell, James B. Use parenthetical identifications in family-heavy works and provide clarifying labels (e.g., Friedman family example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing married women's names
rubrics_metrics.description: A married woman known by birth or married name depending on context should be indexed by her birth name unless the married name is more familiar; women who use both names together are usually indexed by the married name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parenthetical clarifications or cross-references may be supplied as necessary. Examples: Marinoff, Fania (Mrs. Carl Van Vechten); Besant, Annie (née Wood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing monarchs, popes, and official names
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchs, popes, and others known by official names (often with roman numerals) should be indexed under the official name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying tags may be omitted or expanded as relevant. Examples: Anne, Queen; Benedict XVI (pope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing princes, dukes, and titled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes and princesses usually indexed under given names; dukes/earls under title; omit 'Lord' and 'Lady' unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cross-references where title differs from family name. Titles like Sir and Dame are generally unnecessary. Examples illustrate when titles may be used in specialized or historical works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical and academic titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Clerical titles (Rev., Msgr.) used only when necessary for identification; academic titles (Prof., Dr.) and degree abbreviations (PhD, MD) are not retained in indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clerical titles sparingly if needed for identification. Do not retain academic prefixes or degree abbreviations in index entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffixes like Jr., III in index entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations such as Jr. are retained in indexing but are placed after the given name and preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King, Martin Luther, Jr.; Stevenson, Adlai E., III. See also section on punctuation conventions (6.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing saints
rubrics_metrics.description: Saints are indexed under their given names unless another name is equally well or better known; use parenthetical identifications or cross-references as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Thomas Aquinas, Saint; Catherine of Siena, Saint. Use discretion and cross-refs for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing persons whose full names are unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: If persons are referred to by first or last names only in the text, parenthetically identify them if the full name is unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: John (Smith’s shipmate on Stella); Thaxter (family physician). Provide brief identifiers to help readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing incomplete names or epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when an epithet or shortened form of a name is used in the text, the index should give the full form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform 'the lake' into 'Lake Michigan' etc., so the index entry uses the full, standard form for finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing confusing names with identifying tags
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same name refers to more than one entity, provide identifying tags to distinguish (e.g., New York (city) vs New York (state)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide parenthetical clarifications as needed for reader clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing abbreviations and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Widely known organizations by their abbreviations should be indexed and alphabetized under the abbreviation; lesser-known organizations are better indexed under full name with cross-reference from abbreviation if frequently used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add parenthetical glosses or cross-references if abbreviations may not be known to all readers. Examples: EEC (European Economic Community); MLA -> Modern Language Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic treatment for indexed titles of works
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat titles typographically in the index as they appear in the text—italicized, roman with quotes, or capitalized as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply same treatment to newspapers, books, journals, stories, poems, artwork, musical compositions, etc. See 8.156-201 for title typography rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing newspaper titles
rubrics_metrics.description: English-language newspapers are indexed as generally known, The omitted; name italicized; city of publication may be added parenthetically if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York Times; Times (London); for non-English papers include article and optionally city (e.g., Akhbar, Al- (Cairo)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing magazine and journal titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines and journals are indexed like newspapers; omit 'The' for English-language titles, include articles for non-English ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: JAMA; New England Journal of Medicine; Spiegel, Der. Alphabetization rules for articles differ for non-English titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing authored works and relating to creator
rubrics_metrics.description: A work meriting its own main entry should also be indexed under the creator, often as a subentry; main heading followed by creator in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple works by a creator can be subentries under a creator heading or have separate main entries depending on the balance of topics vs works. Examples provided for Mozart and Wolfe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing English-language titles beginning with an article
rubrics_metrics.description: When a title beginning with A, An, or The forms a main heading, the article is traditionally placed at the end of the heading following a comma; as a subheading, it appears in normal position in run-in indexes but inverted in indented indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Professor and the Madman, The (main heading). Inverted forms aid alphabetic scanning in indented indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing non-English titles beginning with an article
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial articles in non-English titles are usually retained in an index; in specialist works, titles may be inverted as in English practice and the article ignored in alphabetizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For general audiences, list titles as in text and alphabetize according to the article. For specialist works, invert (e.g., bohéme, La (Puccini)) and ignore the article in alphabetizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing titles beginning with a preposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepositions at the start of titles always remain in their original position and are not dropped or ignored in alphabetizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For Whom the Bell Tolls; Por quién doblan las campanas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing titles ending with question or exclamation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A question mark or exclamation point at the end of an indexed title should be followed by a comma wherever a comma is called for by the syntax of the heading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Will You Please Be Quiet, Please?, 25-27. See punctuation guidance (6.125) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtitles omitted unless essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtitles of books or articles are omitted in main headings and subheadings unless essential for identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include subtitles when necessary to disambiguate or for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing main headings: first word determines location
rubrics_metrics.description: The first word in a main heading should determine the location of the entry; inversion may be necessary to place titles where readers expect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A Tale of Two Cities -> Tale of Two Cities, A. For subentries follow rules in 16.68-70. Use common-sense adjustments for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computerized sorting caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary word processors' sorting options may not perfectly match Chicago alphabetization; expect to edit sorted output, or use dedicated indexing programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word processors often implement a variation on word-by-word; dedicated indexing software may implement letter-by-letter or word-by-word correctly. Edit the finished product for glitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter-by-letter alphabetizing system
rubrics_metrics.description: In letter-by-letter alphabetizing, sort continuously up to the first parenthesis or comma, then resume after punctuation; spaces and punctuation are ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of precedence: word, word+parenthesis, word+comma, (ignoring spaces/punctuation) word+number, word+letters. Chicago traditionally prefers letter-by-letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-by-word alphabetizing system
rubrics_metrics.description: In word-by-word alphabetizing, alphabetizing continues only up to the end of the first word; subsequent words are used only when headings begin with the same first word; parenthesis/comma interrupt ordering as in letter-by-letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of precedence parallels letter-by-letter but counts whole words first. Use when many open compounds start with same word to ease user scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare letter-by-letter and word-by-word
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand both systems; they share similarities (parenthesis/comma interrupt) but differ in how later characters/words affect order; choose before indexing though change can be applied to entire index if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate differences. Most users scan an alphabetic block and are not confused by either, but indexer must apply chosen system consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing items with same name across categories
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person, place, and thing have the same name, arrange them in normal alphabetical order, using common sense to adjust related entries for reader clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example placing Hoe (garden tool) and Hoe (people) in sensible order; adjust nearby entries if conflicts arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing initials versus spelled-out names
rubrics_metrics.description: Initials used in place of a given name come before any spelled-out name beginning with the same letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Oppenheimer, J. Robert comes before Oppenheimer, James N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing abbreviations and acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms, initialisms, and most abbreviations are alphabetized as they appear, interspersed among entries, not according to their spelled-out versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NATO, FBI, NOW appear in alphabetical order among words. Two exceptions: ampersand may be treated as spelled out; @ may be ignored or treated like 'a' as part of screens/names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing headings beginning with numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated entries beginning with numerals are alphabetized as though the numerals were spelled out; if many numerals occur, they may be listed together numerically at the start of the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1984 alphabetized as 'nineteen eighty-four'; 125th Street as 'one hundred twenty-fifth street'. When similar headings with numerals occur together, order them numerically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing similar headings containing numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more similar headings with numerals occur together, order them numerically regardless of spelled-out form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Henry III, Henry IV, Henry V ordered by roman numeral sequence in L section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing accented letters in English-language indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Words beginning with or including accented letters are alphabetized as though unaccented in English-language indexes that include some non-English words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ubeda, Ubina, Uber den Gipfel treated as if accents absent. For indexes heavy in non-English terms, supplement with Unicode collation rules.
